summary: This note describes phosphenes, the perception of light without light entering the eye. It covers their causes, including mechanical pressure, electrical and magnetic brain stimulation, astronaut radiation exposure, and certain drugs, as well as the proposed mechanism that normal visual-system activity produces them. It also discusses their historical and anthropological significance and research uses such as visual prostheses and the BrainNet brain-to-brain communication experiment.
one_line: Phosphenes are perceived flashes of light without light entering the eye, with causes ranging from pressure and electrical stimulation to radiation and drugs.
key_facts: A phosphene is the phenomenon of seeing light without light entering the eye.
The word phosphene comes from the Greek words phos (light) and phainein (to show).
Pressure phosphenes are caused by rubbing or applying pressure on or near the closed eyes and have been known since antiquity.
Isaac Newton detailed a pressure phosphene in which gently pressing the side of one's eye produces a colored ring of light on the opposite side.
The name 'phosphene' was coined by J. B. H. Savigny, the ship's surgeon of the wrecked French frigate Méduse.
Serre d'Uzes first employed phosphenes to test retinal function prior to cataract surgery.
Neurologist Otfrid Foerster reported phosphenes created by electrical stimulation of the brain as early as 1929.
Brindley and Lewin (1968) inserted a matrix of stimulating electrodes directly into the visual cortex of a 52-year-old blind female to create phosphenes.
Brindley and Rushton (1974) used phosphenes to depict Braille spots as a visual prosthesis.
Astronauts exposed to radiation in space have reported seeing phosphenes.
Patients undergoing radiotherapy have reported seeing blue flashes of light, a phenomenon shown to resemble Cherenkov radiation.
Phosphenes can be caused by some medications, such as Ivabradine.
Most vision researchers believe phosphenes result from normal activity of the visual system after stimulation of one of its parts by a stimulus other than light.

In 1988, David Lewis-Williams and T. A. Dowson argued that non-figurative Upper Paleolithic art depicts visions of phosphenes and neurological 'form constants', probably enhanced by hallucinogenic drugs.
In the BrainNet experiment, five groups of three people each were tested, and the receiver achieved 81% success using phosphenes induced by TMS.
In the BrainNet experiment, senders' EEG signals were tied to flashing lights at 15 Hz and 17 Hz to signal block rotation direction.
